text: SPOTREP 0114/Mar. At 0412Z the coastal radar post at Cape Orlin reported a bulk carrier, MV Karelia Star, steaming south-southeast at 11 knots about 14 nautical miles off the headland. The vessel is Panamanian-flagged and sits low in the water, suggesting a full load. No AIS transmission was received between 0350Z and 0430Z, although the vessel had been broadcasting normally earlier in the watch. The harbour pilot station was not contacted by the ship. The post assesses the AIS gap as probably an equipment fault, low confidence. Observation was by radar and one visual check through the night scope; hull colour was dark blue with a white superstructure.

SPOTREP 0115/Mar. At 0436Z the same post at Cape Orlin tracked a general cargo ship, MV Karelia Sun, heading north-northwest at 8 knots about 9 nautical miles off the headland. The vessel is Liberian-flagged and rides high in the water, suggesting it is empty or lightly loaded. Its AIS was transmitting throughout. The ship called the harbour pilot station at 0441Z and asked for an anchorage berth at the outer roads. The post assesses routine traffic. Observation was by radar and AIS only; weather prevented a visual check. Hull colour could not be determined.

TRACKREP A-41. Air surveillance radar at Ridge Station held track 7731 from 1902Z to 1927Z, a twin-engine turboprop on a steady heading of 070 degrees at 18,000 feet and 240 knots groundspeed. The track squawked a civil transponder code, 4417, and filed no flight plan that the station could find. It passed 22 nautical miles south of the Halvard airstrip without descending. The operator rated the track low interest. Track was lost in ground clutter at 1927Z over the Dunmere hills; no hand-off to the neighbouring sector was made.

TRACKREP A-42. Ridge Station held track 7740 from 1931Z to 1958Z, a single-engine piston aircraft heading 250 degrees at 6,500 feet and 110 knots groundspeed. It squawked 2203 and matched a filed flight plan from Halvard airstrip to Tarn Field. The track descended steadily after 1950Z and was handed off to Tarn Field approach at 1958Z. The operator rated it routine. Radar coverage was good throughout, with no clutter loss.

PATROL SUMMARY 3-12. A road patrol at checkpoint Birch observed a convoy of six trucks and one fuel bowser moving east on Route 9 at 0640 local. Vehicles were painted in a sand pattern and carried no unit markings. The convoy kept roughly 80 metres between vehicles at about 35 km/h. A staff car joined at the rear near the Marl bridge. The patrol photographed the lead truck and the bowser. The convoy did not stop at the checkpoint and could not be challenged, as the patrol had no vehicle to follow. Assessment: probable military logistic movement, medium confidence.

PATROL SUMMARY 3-13. A road patrol at checkpoint Cedar observed a convoy of three buses moving west on Route 4 at 0715 local. The buses were white with a blue stripe and showed the operator name Lindqvist Tours on the side. Spacing was about 40 metres at around 50 km/h. The convoy stopped at the checkpoint, passengers were checked, and all documents were found in order. The patrol photographed the lead bus. Assessment: civilian charter movement, high confidence.

EMITTER NOTE 5-08. Direction-finding site Fenn recorded a pulsed emitter on 9.41 GHz at 2105Z, bearing 315 degrees from the site. Pulse width was 1.2 microseconds with a repetition interval of 1,000 microseconds. The signal was present for 14 minutes before it stopped. Signal strength was strong, suggesting range under 30 kilometres. The parameters match a commercial marine navigation radar. No second site obtained a bearing, so no position fix was possible.

EMITTER NOTE 5-09. Direction-finding site Gorse recorded a pulsed emitter on 3.05 GHz at 2230Z, bearing 040 degrees from the site. Pulse width was 0.8 microseconds with a repetition interval of 2,400 microseconds. The signal was present for 3 minutes. Signal strength was weak. The parameters do not match any entry in the local emitter library. Sites Gorse and Hale both obtained bearings, giving a position fix about 60 kilometres north-east of Gorse.

IMAGERY NOTE 6-21. Satellite pass of 14 March over Kellan airfield, resolution 0.5 metres, cloud cover 10 percent. Compared with the 2 March pass, two hangars were completed on the north apron and a new 300-metre taxiway links the apron to the main runway. Eleven aircraft were visible on the ramp, up from seven. Fuel tanks near the east gate were unchanged. No vehicle activity was seen on the runway. The analyst assesses an expansion of apron capacity, high confidence.

IMAGERY NOTE 6-22. Satellite pass of 14 March over Dorne airfield, resolution 0.5 metres, cloud cover 65 percent. Cloud obscured the southern half, including the runway threshold. Compared with the 2 March pass, the northern ramp showed five aircraft, unchanged, and a perimeter fence was extended by about 200 metres on the west side. One fuel tank near the control tower appeared to have been removed. The analyst assesses no significant change, low confidence because of cloud.

SENSOR LOG 7-03. Coastal radar Cape Orlin was offline from 0200Z to 0545Z on 9 March for scheduled maintenance of the rotary joint. Two technicians replaced a worn bearing and recalibrated azimuth, finishing with an alignment error of 0.2 degrees. Coverage during the outage was provided by the mobile radar at Pike Hill. The radar returned to service at 0545Z and passed the acceptance check on the first attempt.

SENSOR LOG 7-04. Coastal radar Torre Point was offline from 1130Z to 1410Z on 11 March after a lightning strike damaged the transmitter power supply. One technician replaced the supply unit. Azimuth alignment was not affected. No backup radar was available during the outage, leaving a coverage gap in the northern sector. The radar returned to service at 1410Z but failed the acceptance check once and passed on the second attempt.
